content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus treats 'tree' as a polyvalent biblical image with a dominant sense — a person (or people) whose spiritual condition is shown by outward fruit, flourishing when rooted in God — alongside well-attested distinct senses: the Tree of Life (eternal life/paradise), the cross of Christ as 'the tree,' great trees as kingdoms/empires/rulers, Israel as fig/olive tree, and the mustard-seed kingdom tree. Three of four responses stress there is no single settled meaning; context determines which sense applies.","book_summary":"The book defines the tree as a single unified symbol: a rooted covenant life known by its fruit, which scales continuously from one planted seed or person up to a house, lineage, people, or nation; mature branches are individual members who may shelter others, and the fruit becomes seed for further growth.","consensus_core_identification":"A tree is primarily a person or people whose inner spiritual state is made visible in fruit, with separate additional senses (Tree of Life, cross, kingdoms, Israel) applied according to context.","book_core_identification":"A tree is one scalable symbol of covenant life known by its fruit — the same image applying at every scale from individual person to lineage, people, or nation, with branches as members.","core_relation":"BOOK_BROADENS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book merges what the consensus keeps as distinct senses. The consensus separates the individual righteous tree (Ps 1, Jer 17), the kingdom/empire tree (Dan 4, Ezek 17/31), Israel as olive/fig tree (Rom 11), and the mustard-seed kingdom tree; the book reclassifies all of these as one continuous symbol differing only in scale. Conversely, the book omits or excludes senses the consensus rates dominant or common: the Tree of Life as eternal life, and the cross of Christ as 'the tree.' The 'covenant' qualifier also sits awkwardly with Daniel 4, where the consensus reads the tree as a pagan king's dominion rather than covenant life.","material_contradiction":"None at the core. The book does not deny that trees can represent persons or nations; it asserts these are the same symbol at different scales and adds structural details (branches = members, fruit = seed for propagation) that the consensus does not assert but does not contradict.","rationale":"The book preserves the consensus's central referent — a rooted life (personal or corporate) known by its fruit — so the cores overlap substantially rather than contradict. But it materially changes the boundary: it unifies the individual-tree, kingdom-tree, Israel-tree, and mustard-seed senses into one scalable meaning (a claim Response A explicitly flags as beyond mainstream consensus), reclassifies kingdom-trees as scaled covenant life, and drops the Tree of Life and cross senses that the consensus treats as dominant/common. This is real boundary disagreement without replacement of the central identification, fitting REFINED with BOOK_BROADENS at the core and PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION at the extension.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"The printed citations do trace a coherent scale — planted individual (Ps 1:3), fruit-known character (Luke 6:43-45), one person increased into a people (Isa 51:2), planted twig growing into a sheltering cedar (Ezek 17:22-24), seed into kingdom-tree (Matt 13:31-32), and branches as grafted members (Rom 11:17) — so one could argue the unified reading is strongly supported and closer to MATCH with the consensus's dominant sense. However, Dan 4:22 (Nebuchadnezzar's pagan dominion) strains the 'covenant life' framing, Isa 51:2 contains no tree imagery at all, and the citations cannot establish that the Tree of Life and cross senses are properly subsumed or excluded; the unification itself is asserted rather than demonstrated by the printed verses.","confidence":"high"}
